AccessKeyCreated.description:
The ``201`` body -- **the only time the secret is ever returned**.

``201`` rather than ``202`` is not this module's invention: the frozen v1
contract already records it as the sync exception to §9 item 1, for the same
reason ``domain/access_keys.py`` arrives at independently -- the result is a
secret, and a secret cannot be handed over asynchronously without being
stored.

``secret_access_key`` is optional in the schema for one reason: an
idempotent replay. A repeated request carrying the same ``Idempotency-Key``
gets the stored response back, and the stored response has the secret
stripped -- because storing it would be the at-rest copy this whole design
exists to avoid. So a replay returns the same key with
``secret_access_key: null``, which is the honest answer: the credential
exists, and its secret is gone.

secret_access_key.description: The plaintext secret. Shown once and never retrievable again -- nothing stores it. Save it now. null on an idempotent replay.
secret_access_key.title: Secret Access Key

AccessKeyOut.description:
An S3 access key's **metadata**. There is no field for the secret.

Not an oversight and not a redaction: the plaintext is never stored, so this
model could not expose it even if someone added a field. The only place it
ever exists is the ``201`` body of the request that minted it.

``rgw_access_key_id`` is the *public* half -- the value that goes in an
``Authorization`` header and appears in the object store's own access log.
It is an identifier, not a credential, and a customer needs it to know which
of their keys a row refers to.

**The field names come from the frozen v1 contract**
(``docs/openapi/openapi-customer-v1.yaml``), not from this module's own
taste. ``BucketOut`` deliberately hides provider coordinates, and by that
habit this would be ``access_key_id`` -- but the contract the panel's
generated client is written against says ``rgw_access_key_id``, and the
value genuinely is one a customer pastes into their own tooling rather than
an internal name. Matching the contract exactly is what stops a
reconciliation nobody scheduled.

openbao_path.description: Deprecated: always null, and will be removed in v2. The secret is shown once, in the `201` body that minted it, and is held nowhere else.
openbao_path.title: Openbao Path

rgw_access_key_id.description: The public half of the credential. null while it is still being issued.

account. A customer may know the name of the plan they are on; whether it
is the platform default, or what a *different* plan would grant, is not
theirs to read from this surface (see
``customer_api/routes/billing.py::_price_out``'s docstring for the same
boundary drawn around price fields).

the admin-editable label and carries no other meaning

The only billing field a customer sets directly -- everything else on

rather than left to the column's own ``CHECK``

BucketQuotaOut.description:
A bucket's storage ceiling.

``null`` in a dimension means *this bucket is not individually capped* --
not "unlimited". The organization's own ceiling still applies above it, so a
client rendering "unlimited" here would be telling the customer something
the platform never promised.

BucketQuotaRequest.description:
``PUT /v1/orgs/{org}/s3/buckets/{bucket_id}/quota``.

Each dimension has three requests, not two: a number sets a cap, ``null``
removes one, and *omitting the key* leaves that dimension exactly as it is.
The "leave this alone" sentinel a ``PATCH`` would need already exists --
it is ``model_fields_set``, which is how the handler tells a ``None`` the
client sent from the ``None`` this field defaults to.

Reading an omitted field as ``null`` instead is P1-45: a body carrying only
``max_objects`` silently cleared the bucket's size ceiling, and a body whose
only key was misspelled cleared both, each with a ``202``. Unknown keys are
now refused outright (see ``RequestModel``), which removes the second case;
this class's semantics remove the first.

The method stays ``PUT`` rather than becoming ``PATCH``. It is idempotent
and the path addresses the quota resource itself, which is what ``PUT``
requires; a merge-patch body is not by itself a reason to change the verb
on a frozen v1 contract.

max_objects.description: Objects this bucket may hold. Send null for no per-bucket cap; omit to leave this dimension unchanged.
max_objects.title: Max Objects

max_size_bytes.description: Bytes this bucket may hold. Must fit inside your organization's ceiling. Send null to remove the per-bucket cap -- the organization ceiling still applies. Omit to leave this dimension unchanged.
max_size_bytes.title: Max Size Bytes

BucketQuotaRequest.title: BucketQuotaRequest

these are counts read straight off the storage backend and are exact as
integers. Sending them as strings would imply a precision question that
does not exist here.

A minted console, handed over once.

``url`` is a single-use link, so this body **is** the credential: it is
returned exactly once per operation and never again -- a second poll gets a
404. Open it immediately and do not persist it; it is not cached and not
logged, for the same reason ``VmOut`` publishes no detail of how this
platform builds a VM -- this surface hands over what the customer holds,
not how the console was minted.

``expires_in_seconds`` is this platform's own floor, not a value it merely
relays, so a panel can stop offering a link it already knows is stale
rather than opening a tab onto an expired one.

sent (only the lines containing it are in ``output``) and is ``null`` when none was; it is a
convenience for picking your own lines out of a noisy log, not an access boundary.
``size_bytes`` is the length of ``output`` in UTF-8 bytes.

One rule as a customer's ``PUT`` sends it.

Deliberately the request half of ``domain.compute.edge.FirewallRuleIn``
rather than that dataclass reused directly: that one carries no field
validation of its own (mirroring migration 0038's CHECK constraints is
``edge._validate_rule``'s job, not this shape's), and a body model needs
``RequestModel``'s ``extra="forbid"`` plus its unstorable-text guard, which
a plain dataclass has neither of.

``port_min``/``port_max`` carry only the ``Integer`` column's ``int32``
overflow ceiling here (P0-27's second crash class -- see
``VmCreateRequest``'s docstring for the same reasoning applied to
``vcpus``/``memory_mb``/``disk_gb``): the actual business rule -- present
together for ``tcp``/``udp``, absent together for ``icmp``/``any``, and
``1..65535`` -- is ``edge._validate_rule``'s, which reports it with an
indexed, per-rule message a blanket field bound cannot.

client that forgot the field -- rather than one that deliberately asked to
clear its firewall -- silently wipe every rule on the VM, the same
P1-45-shaped hazard ``NotificationPreferencesRequest`` documents for its own
single required field.

No ``max_length`` on the list: :data:`MAX_FIREWALL_RULES` is
``edge.py``'s business rule, reported with a message naming the count sent
and the ceiling, and a pydantic-level cap would pre-empt it with a bare
``400`` for the one scenario ``tests/api/test_compute_mutations.py``
actually names.

InvitationOut.description:
An invitation, as an org's owners/admins see it -- never the token.

``state`` and ``joined`` are both derived, never stored columns (D-R6-3):
see ``domain.invitations.invitation_state``. ``joined`` answers a
different question from ``state == "redeemed"`` -- redemption
(``accepted_at``, R6-T3) happens the moment the link is used; binding
(``accepted_by_sub``, also R6-T3) happens later, at the invitee's first
login with a verified matching email. An invitation can therefore be

across hours nothing measured. Summing per-bucket points would produce a
number that looks like money and is not.

info.description:
Customer API for VirtScale compute and object storage (public, api.virtscale.nl). Everything is scoped to an organization: `/v1/orgs/{org}/...`.
- Auth: `Authorization: Bearer <credential>`, a customers-realm JWT or an organization API token (`vsk_...`). Only the health probes, `GET /v1/status`, the Stripe webhook and invitation redeem are open.
- Discover first: `GET /v1/orgs/{org}/capabilities` lists what this credential may do, the route and permission each needs, and whether it is switched on (`available`, `unavailable_reason`).
- Errors: every non-2xx body is `application/problem+json` (`ProblemDetail`). Branch on `code`, never on `detail`. A malformed request is `400 invalid_request` with `errors[{field,message}]`; a well-formed request that is refused (quota, plan, VM state, a switch that is off) is 409, 422 or 503 with its own code.
- Error registry: `docs/capabilities/compute.json` in the repository lists every compute error `code` with its status, category, whether the same request may succeed later (`retryable`) and the `remedy`, and the `error_class` values of failed operations.
- Async: a mutation answers `202` with a `Location` header naming the operation (`/v1/orgs/{org}/operations/{id}`). Poll it until `state` is `succeeded`, `failed` or `cancelled`.
- Rate limits: a caller that sends too many requests per second, counted by source address and by organization, gets `429 rate_limited` with a `Retry-After` header (whole seconds); wait that long and send the request again. The health probes are never limited.
- `Idempotency-Key` is honoured on every mutation of the compute, project, member, budget, quota, notification and S3 routes, except the few that mint something single-use (a console, a billing portal session, an API token) and the invitation redeem. The same key with the same request replays the first answer; with another body or another resource it is `409 idempotency_key_reused`.
- Only some lists page by cursor: the VM lists, the public-IP lists, the invoice list and the audit log take `limit` and `cursor` and return `next_cursor`, null on the last page. The operation lists take `limit` only.
info.title: VirtScale Cloud API

get.description:
Liveness probe. No dependency calls -- process-up check only.

Liveness failure means *restart this container*, so it must never depend on
anything a restart cannot fix. A liveness probe wired to the database turns
a database blip into a rolling restart of every pod that talks to it, which
is how a recoverable outage becomes an unrecoverable one.

Readiness probe: real DB + MQ + JWKS checks, gated on configuration.

Each dependency's check is gated purely by whether ``settings.Settings``
has that dependency configured --

    settings.database_url            unset -> "db" key omitted
    settings.amqp_url                unset -> "mq" key omitted
    settings.kc_customers_issuer_url
    settings.kc_staff_issuer_url     both unset -> "jwks" key omitted

plus, for the worker only, ``app.state.expects_consumer`` /
``app.state.consumer``. An API pod sets neither and omits the key. A worker
that has committed to consuming sets the first immediately and the second
once the consumer exists, so the key reads ``false`` for the whole of
startup and ``true`` only while it is genuinely consuming -- the difference
between "this pod executes operations" and "this pod is a process that
publishes reaper messages into a queue nobody drains".

An unconfigured dependency is never reported as failing -- omitted, not
``false`` -- so a service deployed before all three land degrades
gracefully instead of never reaching Ready. Once a dependency's URL is set,
its check becomes mandatory and runs on every probe.

**What a check observes and what it decides are two different things.**
``checks`` reports what was observed; the status code reports what that is
allowed to do about this pod's place in its Service. They agree for every
dependency this pod can be individually responsible for, and they can
disagree for one shared by every replica -- because withdrawing every
replica of an API over a dependency none of them can influence removes the
API without moving a single request anywhere useful. So the three shapes
are:

    200 ``{"status": "ok",       "checks": {...all true...}}``
    200 ``{"status": "degraded", "checks": {...}}``  something is wrong,
         and it is not something taking this pod out of the Service fixes
    503 ``{"status": "degraded", "checks": {...}}``  this pod, specifically,
         should not receive traffic

``readiness.py`` documents what counts as a *real* failure per dependency,
which failures are allowed to decide (``decides_readiness``), and in
particular why neither an unreachable Keycloak nor -- after this process has
once reached them -- an unreachable shared PostgreSQL or RabbitMQ is one.
The routes that need those dependencies answer ``503 problem+json`` with a
``Retry-After`` while this endpoint reports ``200 degraded``; that pairing
is the whole reason the pod is worth keeping in its Service.

The body is booleans only. Probe bodies are not shown by ``kubectl describe
pod`` and there is no reason to risk a DSN or an internal hostname reaching
a log aggregator through one -- the reason a check failed is logged
instead.

post.description:
Start a Checkout Session, guarded so a client's retry cannot double-charge intent.

Ordering: deployment-config gates first (cheapest, no DB dependency of
their own beyond what ``org_session`` already opened), then the 404, then
the ``billing_exempt`` refusal, then the idempotency replay (so a stored
409/503 from an earlier attempt with the same key replays correctly --
see ``IdempotencyGuard.replay``), then the two remaining business gates,
then :func:`_orphan_precheck`, then the actual Stripe call. The pre-check
sits last among the gates because it is itself a Stripe round trip: it
answers "is this org already paying at Stripe even though no local row says
so", which the local ``state``/``stripe_customer_id`` pair cannot, and a
``409 billing_subscription_orphaned`` from it means something a
``billing_already_active`` does not -- see that function. That 409 also
covers the case where Stripe returns a subscription for this org whose
status this service does not recognise: an unreadable status is refused
rather than read as "nothing is being charged", because a subscription
object coming back is itself the evidence that one exists.

``billing_exempt`` is checked *before* ``guard.replay`` claims anything:
an exempt org is staff-managed and must fail closed on every attempt --
not just the first one to claim a given ``Idempotency-Key``. Refusing
ahead of the claim means there is nothing here for a later retry to
replay: once staff lifts the exemption, the identical request (same key
included) reaches Stripe normally instead of forever replaying a stale
409. See :func:`_deny_billing_exempt`.

A Stripe outage answers ``503 stripe_unreachable`` (design doc §15) and
**releases the key this request claimed**, so the customer's retry runs
for real instead of meeting ``409 idempotency_in_progress`` for 24 hours.
See the explicit ``rollback`` at the call site for why that is written out
rather than left to the dependency teardown.

``billing_already_active`` refusal -- adding or replacing a card is always
allowed, even when one is already attached. A Stripe outage answers
``503 stripe_unreachable`` and releases the claimed key, as the checkout
route does.

put.description:
Switch this VM's protection against deletion on or off.

While it is on, deleting the VM answers ``409 vm_protected`` -- to everybody,
this organization's owners included -- so a VM that must not disappear by
accident cannot. It changes nothing about the VM itself: no restart, no
operation, nothing in the cloud, which is why this answers ``200`` with the
VM rather than ``202``. Every switch, in either direction, is audited.

**Governed by IAM like every other route** (the AWS ``ModifyInstanceAttribute``
``DisableApiTermination`` shape): the router-wide permission check admits whoever
holds ``compute.instance.update`` -- the owner, admin and member roles, and an API
key with the ``write`` or ``compute:write`` scope, so a Terraform key sets and lifts
protection itself -- and anyone else is ``403 permission_denied``. There is no
owner-only rule and no lifecycle switch. The permission is checked again inside this
handler, so it holds with ``S3CP_IAM_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED`` off, when the router-wide
gate only logs: the check is fail-closed and audited like the gate's own refusals.

compute mutations are off.

``protection`` (``domain/compute/vm_actions.py``): a VM in a region whose
disks are single copies on one host -- HEL -- is protected or not as staff
decided, in either direction, because lifting it would hand the VM its stop
and reboot back.

The switch itself -- the locked read, the policy, the write and the audit row --
is ``vms.set_vm_protection``, which the staff route calls too. It answers after
the mutations flag and the permission check, and before anything is written.

than from its own disk, which stays attached so it can be repaired -- the
way back from a VM that no longer boots. It stays in rescue until it is
unrescued, which restarts it once more, from its own disk.

``202``, like every other mutation here. What commits is a ``vm.rescue``
operation and nothing on the VM; the executor settles it in ``rescued``.

the guest shuts down cleanly -- and it is refused for the same reasons: a
server that is stopped at that moment, or busy with another change, is not
restarted, and the schedule records why.

than run late: nobody wants a maintenance restart hours after the window
they chose.

put.description:
Switch this VM's protection against deletion on or off.

While it is on, deleting the VM answers ``409 vm_protected`` -- to everybody,
this organization's owners included -- so a VM that must not disappear by
accident cannot. It changes nothing about the VM itself: no restart, no
operation, nothing in the cloud, which is why this answers ``200`` with the
VM rather than ``202``. Every switch, in either direction, is audited.

**Governed by IAM like every other route** (the AWS ``ModifyInstanceAttribute``
``DisableApiTermination`` shape): the router-wide permission check admits whoever
holds ``compute.instance.update`` -- the owner, admin and member roles, and an API
key with the ``write`` or ``compute:write`` scope, so a Terraform key sets and lifts
protection itself -- and anyone else is ``403 permission_denied``. There is no
owner-only rule and no lifecycle switch. The permission is checked again inside this
handler, so it holds with ``S3CP_IAM_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED`` off, when the router-wide
gate only logs: the check is fail-closed and audited like the gate's own refusals.

compute mutations are off.

``protection`` (``domain/compute/vm_actions.py``): a VM in a region whose
disks are single copies on one host -- HEL -- is protected or not as staff
decided, in either direction, because lifting it would hand the VM its stop
and reboot back.

The switch itself -- the locked read, the policy, the write and the audit row --
is ``vms.set_vm_protection``, which the staff route calls too. It answers after
the mutations flag and the permission check, and before anything is written.

creating buckets. §7.4 puts ``suspended -> active`` behind admin ``restore``

post.description:
Issue a credential scoped to this organization's storage tenant.

The secret appears in this response body and nowhere else, ever. Nothing
stores it -- not a column, not the audit trail, not the operation row -- so
there is no recovery path by design: a client that loses it revokes this key
and creates another.

**The credential is a key on the organization's own RGW owner user.** It can
therefore delete this organization's buckets and objects directly over S3,
bypassing the soft-delete window and the audit trail this API provides. That
is a real cost of issuing it and it is spelled out in
``domain/access_keys.py``, in the README and in the endpoint's OpenAPI
description rather than left to be discovered.

``Idempotency-Key`` is honoured, and its interaction with the once-only rule
is the interesting part. The stored response has the secret **stripped**
before it is written, so a replayed request returns the same credential's
metadata with a null secret rather than re-exposing the plaintext from a
JSONB column. Retrying the request is safe; it just cannot un-lose the
secret. Without a key, a retry mints a second credential -- which is the
correct behaviour for a non-idempotent mint and the reason the header is
worth sending.

A key whose request was *refused* replays the refusal rather than answering
``409 idempotency_in_progress`` forever -- except for a ``5xx``, where the
claim is released so the retry the client was told to make actually runs.
See ``db.idempotency``.
post.summary: Create an S3 access key (the secret is returned exactly once)

delete.description:
Begin revoking a credential.

``202``, not ``204``: the credential is still live in the object store when
this returns, and the operation in the body is how a customer knows when it
genuinely stopped working. For a *leaked* key that distinction is the whole
answer to "am I safe yet?", and a ``204`` would give them no way to ask.

Another org's key id yields ``404``, not ``403`` -- RLS filters the row out,
so the handler cannot tell "someone else's" from "nobody's" (§5).

Takes an ``Idempotency-Key`` (PROV-009): a retry gets the first answer back, with the same
operation to poll, instead of a refusal for a key that is already being revoked.

get.description:
Every bucket this organization owns.

RLS already restricts the rows to the caller's org; the domain query
filters again. Belt and braces, and cheap -- the index is on
``(org_id, state)`` either way.

post.description:
Accept a bucket creation and start converging it.

Always ``202``, never ``201`` (§3.3 row 13): the resource is not ready when
this returns, and saying ``201`` would be a lie that clients would build
optimistic UI on top of. The ``Location`` header points at the operation to
poll.

Ordering, which is the whole reason this is not three lines: the bucket row,
the operation row and the audit row commit **together**; only then is the
dispatch message published; only then is ``published_at`` stamped. Publish
inside the transaction and a worker can pick up a bucket that never
committed. See ``mq/publisher``.

**Two ceilings refuse here, both ``422``**, since 2026-09-04 (P0-26).
``bucket_limit_reached`` means the org has no free ``max_buckets`` slot; a
soft-deleted bucket no longer holds one, so the delete the detail asks for
genuinely frees a slot, and the detail names how many deletes it takes
rather than assuming one. ``bucket_retention_limit_reached`` is the new
code: too many bucket rows in total -- live plus soft-deleted -- against
``2 x max_buckets``, a ceiling that exists because the first no longer
bounds how many buckets an org can cause to *exist*. Its detail never says
"delete one" (deleting adds a row to the total it measures) and never says
"wait" (erasure is the purge worker's job, and that worker ships disabled,
so an elapsed window permits a purge rather than causing one).

**What that detail names depends on this deployment** (P1-59, 2026-09-05).
Where nothing erases -- ``S3CP_BUCKET_PURGE_ENABLED`` false, which is the
shipped setting and production's, or the loop idled with
``S3CP_BUCKET_PURGE_INTERVAL_SECONDS`` at ``0``, which is the documented
incident lever -- the ceiling has no drain, so the detail says so and
quotes no erasure date; where the purge worker runs, it names the date the
oldest row becomes eligible. That claim is composed from **this pod's**
environment while the erasing is the worker pod's, so it holds only while
the two deployments carry the same value -- see the service README's
"env parity" note under §4.5. Neither version offers a plan upgrade: this
product has no plan tier, and the only thing that raises ``max_buckets`` is
an admin ``quota_overrides`` row, so the second move it names is asking
support. The customer-side move -- restore one of the soft-deleted buckets
-- is available in both, because the slot check refuses first and reaching
this ceiling therefore implies a free slot.

**``versioning`` is now applied, and was not until 2026-09-05 (P1-54).**
The flag was accepted, stored and echoed back on every read while no
``PutBucketVersioning`` ever reached the object store, so a customer who
ticked the box believing overwrites were recoverable was wrong and every
read agreed with them. The ``bucket.create`` operation this returns now
applies it and records what the store then reported in
``observed_versioning``; a store that will not hold it fails the operation
rather than closing it ``succeeded`` over a bucket that cannot honour the
promise. There is still no route that *changes* versioning after the
create -- ``PUT .../versioning`` is P2 in the frozen contract and is not
implemented here.
post.summary: Create a bucket

delete.description:
Soft-delete: cut access, start the retention clock, keep the data.

Nothing is destroyed here **and nothing is destroyed by the operation this
returns**. The bucket enters ``deleting_soft`` with a ``purge_after``
``S3CP_BUCKET_PURGE_RETENTION_DAYS`` (7) in the future; the worker makes
the data unreachable and deletes nothing; erasure happens only once the
window elapses, as a separate ``bucket.purge`` operation.
``POST .../restore`` cancels it until then.

Until 2026-09-02 that was a promise this docstring made and the executor
broke -- it deleted at RGW immediately, and ``?force=true`` erased every
object. See ``domain.buckets.delete_bucket``.

``?force=true`` acknowledges that the bucket may be non-empty (§4.5); it is
audited and it authorises nothing destructive.

``409 bucket_not_empty`` when the bucket is not empty and ``?force=true``
was not given. Corrected 2026-09-04 (P1-42b): §4.5 has always required the
acknowledgement for a non-empty bucket, but nothing read an object count,
so the flag was decorative.

"Not empty" is judged from the **most recent metering sample**, not from a
fresh call to the object store: the sampler already records a per-bucket
object and byte count for every org every
``S3CP_METERING_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_SECONDS`` (600 s), and the API deliberately
reaches the provider in exactly one place (the access-key mint). So the
observation is up to that interval stale, in both directions, and the
refusal states the timestamp it was made at rather than implying a fresh
look. On a **versioned** bucket the refusal says so explicitly, because the
sample counts every version the store holds while the customer's own
``ListObjectsV2`` shows only current ones -- so "I deleted everything" and
"the measurement found five objects" are both true at the same time, and a
409 that did not explain that would read as the API contradicting the
customer's own evidence. An org with no sample yet -- or whose sampler has stopped -- is not
refused: absent evidence must not make ``?force=true`` mandatory for every
delete, since a customer who cannot pay has to be able to stop the meter.

``?force=true`` still never travels in the message, so a delete recovered
by the reaper (which republishes type and operation id only) behaves
identically to the original request.

parameters.description: Acknowledge that the bucket may still contain objects and soft-delete it anyway (§4.5). Required when the most recent metering observation of this bucket saw objects or bytes in it; without it that delete is `409 bucket_not_empty`. This does **not** erase anything and does not shorten the retention window -- it is recorded in the audit trail as an explicit acknowledgement.

get.description:
One bucket by its VirtScale id.

Another org's bucket id yields ``404``, not ``403``: RLS filters the row
out, so the handler genuinely cannot tell "someone else's" from "nobody's"
-- and must not pretend otherwise (§5 Status codes).

put.description:
Set this bucket's storage ceiling, within the organization's own.

``202``, not ``200``: the object store has not been told when this returns.
Reporting success would let a client render "you now have 10 TB" for a
ceiling that is not in force yet, and the ``Location`` header is how it
learns when it is.

A request above the organization's effective ceiling (plan plus any live
override) is refused ``422`` with ``bucket_quota_exceeds_plan`` and the
refusal is audited. A ``null`` dimension removes the *per-bucket* cap; the
organization's ceiling still binds above it, which is why removing one is
not a way around the plan.

**An omitted dimension is left unchanged; an explicit ``null`` clears it.**
Those are different requests and the body distinguishes them, so the
handler must too: ``model_fields_set`` is the only place that knows whether
a ``None`` came from the client or from the field's default, and once the
two are collapsed nothing downstream can tell them apart again. Getting
this wrong is P1-45 -- a ``PUT`` carrying only ``max_objects`` wiped the
bucket's size ceiling, because "absent" was read as "remove it". A client
editing one dimension has no reason to know the other's current value, and
making it send one back would be a read-modify-write race for no gain.

**An empty body ``{}`` follows from that rule and is a ``202`` no-op**: no
dimension was supplied, so neither changes. It is not free, and the cost is
stated here rather than discovered: it still opens an operation, which
takes this bucket's one in-flight slot (§9 item 8) and makes the client's
*next* ``PUT`` a ``409`` until a worker drains it, still writes an audit row
whose ``before`` equals its ``after``, and still re-converges the stored
quota to RGW. Before P1-45 the same body cleared both dimensions, so this
is strictly the safer answer -- but a client with nothing to change should
send no request at all.

post.description:
Take a soft delete back, inside its retention window.

``202``, like every other mutation here: the retention clock is stopped in
the transaction that answers this, but the object store has not been told
to serve the bucket again when the response is written, so reporting
``200`` would tell a customer their data was reachable a moment before it
was. The ``Location`` header is how they learn when it is.

``409 bucket_not_deleting`` when the bucket is not scheduled for deletion
-- there is nothing to cancel. ``409 bucket_purge_in_progress`` only when
erasure has actually begun (the row is ``purging``), which is a different
answer and is coded separately: the data may be gone. Another
organization's bucket id, and one that has already been purged, are both
``404`` (§5 Status codes) -- ``403`` would confirm the bucket exists.

``422 bucket_limit_reached`` when the org has no free ``max_buckets`` slot,
new 2026-09-04 (P0-26) and easy to miss on a route whose point is that a
mistaken delete stays recoverable. A soft-deleted bucket no longer holds a
slot, so a restore *takes one back* and has to be admitted like a create.
The detail names how many buckets have to be deleted first -- more than one
for an org sitting above its effective ceiling after a plan downgrade or a
lapsed quota override.

Corrected 2026-09-04 (P0-26): an elapsed ``purge_after`` on its own no
longer refuses. It used to answer ``409 bucket_purge_window_elapsed`` with
"its data is being or has been erased", which on a deployment running the
shipped ``S3CP_BUCKET_PURGE_ENABLED=false`` was false -- nothing had been
erased, because the purge worker never ran. An elapsed window means a purge
is permitted, not that one happened.

Takes an ``Idempotency-Key`` (PROV-009). Without one, the one-in-flight rule collapses a
retry into ``409 operation_in_flight`` while the first restore is converging, and a restore
that has *finished* leaves the bucket ``active``, where a repeat is refused
``bucket_not_deleting``. With one, a retry of the same request gets the first answer back.
post.summary: Cancel a soft delete and restore access

get.description:
The endpoint(s) a client should point its S3 SDK at.

Static and DB-free -- one region, path-style addressing, because the
platform serves exactly one today. The list envelope (rather than a bare
object) is what lets a second region or addressing style arrive later as
an additional item instead of a breaking response-shape change.

Reads ``request.app.state.settings`` rather than ``get_settings()``: the
latter re-reads the environment on every call, which would ignore
whatever ``Settings`` instance the app was actually built with (tests
construct one directly, with no environment involved at all).
get.summary: List published S3 endpoints and addressing styles

get.description:
The price book, readable **before** this org has enabled anything.

This is the one billing read that must not be gated on a
``billing_accounts`` row. That row is seeded by ``enable_s3`` (§6.2), so
every other route in this module answers ``404 not_enabled`` without it --
which is correct for "what is *my* account doing" and exactly wrong for
"what would this cost me". Until this route existed the prices lived only
inside ``GET /billing``, so a prospective customer was asked to press
"Enable Object Storage" with no way to find out the price first.

``GET /billing``'s 404 is deliberately left alone: the panel and
``TestGetBilling`` both depend on it, and it doubles as the answer to "has
this org enabled S3". Prices are simply also served here, unconditionally.

Same item shape as ``BillingOut.prices`` -- literally
:class:`BillingPriceOut`, not a parallel model, so the panel renders a
price identically before and after checkout and there is one definition to
keep in step with the table. Wrapped in the standard list envelope for the
reason :class:`ListResponse` gives: a third meter arriving later is then an
extra item rather than a response-shape break.

**Reads the table, never a literal.** ``unit_amount_micro_eur`` is an open
commercial decision that will move (§0 D8; Asana P0-17), and the bootstrap
ceremony changes it with an ``UPDATE`` -- a constant compiled in here would
become a false quote the moment it did. An empty table therefore answers
``{"items": []}``: honest, and the panel is required to render that as "no
published price" rather than as free.

Org-scoped like every other route on this surface -- ``require_org`` and an
RLS-bound session -- even though ``billing_prices`` has no RLS to bind
(§0 D8: one platform price book, every org sold at the same two prices).
Keeping it inside the org-scoped router costs nothing and means the day a
price becomes org-specific, the caller already passes the org.
get.summary: List the unit prices S3 is sold at

get.description: The org's ceilings and current standing. See ``_read_quota`` for the shape.
get.summary: Get committed/soft/hard quota and current burst state

put.description:
Set ``hard_bytes``; ``soft_bytes`` (the alerting threshold) is derived as
``hard_bytes * 4 // 5`` and is not independently settable.

``200``, not ``202``: unlike a bucket's per-bucket ceiling (RGW-enforced,
``domain/buckets.py::set_bucket_quota``), the org ceiling this endpoint
writes is ``quotas.hard_bytes`` itself -- the row the phase B3 autoscale
reconciler reads *as* the effective ceiling on its own next tick. There is
no backend round trip to wait for here, so reporting success synchronously
is not the lie it would be on the bucket path.

``hard_bytes`` must fall between ``settings.autoscale_floor_bytes`` and
``settings.platform_max_hard_bytes``, inclusive on both ends -- the exact
range ``settings.py`` reserved for this route ahead of it existing. A
``quota_overrides`` row may still exceed ``platform_max_hard_bytes``: that
ceiling is a self-service limit, not the admin escape hatch overrides
exist to be.

**Lowering below current usage is allowed.** The autoscale reconciler
already treats "ceiling below usage" as a legal, if noisy, state --
``autoscale/formula.py`` freezes the enforced quota rather than erroring --
so this route does not refuse it either. The response instead carries
``warning='below_current_usage'`` so a client can render that consequence
without the request itself failing: writes stop once the *enforced* number
(unchanged until the reconciler's next tick) catches down to it, existing
data is untouched, and raising ``hard_bytes`` again reverses it. No
warning -- and no comparison at all -- when this org has never been
sampled: an absent sample is a gap, not a zero usage figure to compare
against.

Audited exactly like ``domain/buckets.py::set_bucket_quota``: one
``quota.set`` row per call, ``before``/``after`` carrying the two changed
columns. Takes an ``Idempotency-Key`` (PROV-009): a retry gets the first answer back and
writes no second audit row.
put.summary: Set the organization's hard storage ceiling

get.description:
Metered usage for this org, bucketed by ``granularity``.

``series`` is read straight off ``usage_hourly`` via
``metering.usage.org_usage_series`` -- the same function phase B1's
Stripe reporter and ``GET /billing`` will read from, so this endpoint and
money never disagree about what happened in a given hour. ``totals`` sums
the series that is actually returned rather than calling
``month_to_date``: the two only coincide when the window *is* the current
month, and a caller asking for last quarter should not get this month's
number back.

parameters.description: Window start (inclusive). Default: start of the current UTC month.

get.description:
Per-bucket storage footprint for this org, bucketed by ``granularity``.

**Usage insight, not billing.** The sibling ``GET .../s3/usage`` reads
``usage_hourly`` -- the integrated, carried-forward quantities Stripe is
told -- and that table has no bucket dimension at all. This reads
``usage_samples``, instantaneous readings taken every 600 s. The two answer
different questions and will not add up to each other; the response carries
no ``totals`` precisely so nothing here can be mistaken for an invoice
line.

**The window ceilings are the data's, not this route's.** ``usage_samples``
is pruned at 35 days, so a longer request cannot be answered -- it would
return a series that simply stops, and a chart cannot tell "purged by
retention" from "the bucket was empty". Hourly granularity is capped
tighter, at 7 days, for response size: the sampler writes every 600 s, so
35 days of hourly points multiplied by every bucket is a payload nobody can
render. ``retention_days`` is returned so a client can cap its own date
picker rather than discovering the limit as a 422.

Defaults to the last 7 days at ``day`` granularity -- the sibling route
defaults to month-to-date, which would exceed the retention ceiling on any
day after the 5th and 422 on its own default.
get.summary: Get per-bucket footprint over a time window

post.description:
Record this organization's acceptance of the current Terms of Service, Privacy Policy and Acceptable Use Policy. Send **all three** documents, each at its current version (as `GET /v1/legal-documents` reports it). Owner and admin only -- accepting a contract is a human act, so an API key cannot do it.

`409 terms_version_stale` names the documents whose version moved. `422 invalid_request` for a list that is empty, incomplete, unknown or repeated. `201` when this call recorded an acceptance; `200` when every current document was already accepted (the response is the same either way). An acceptance is append-only and the **first** acceptor's row is kept, so a second acceptance of the same version changes nothing. An optional `Idempotency-Key` replays the stored response.

post.description:
Create a VPC in this project and return `202` with the operation to poll.

Always `202`: nothing exists when this returns, and the `Location` header names the
operation to follow. Every refusal a request can provoke is decided before anything is
queued, with a `code` to act on: `409 name_taken` when this project already has a live
VPC of that name in that region, `409 vpc_address_space_exhausted` when no block of the
requested size is free, `422 quota_exceeded` when the organization has spent its
allowance, `422 region_unavailable` for a region that is not available to you,
`422 vpc_not_available` for one that does not offer VPCs, `422 invalid_spec` for a
block size the address plan does not allow, `422 invalid_name` for a name that is not
a valid label, `409 compute_not_enabled` while the organization is not enrolled,
`409 operation_in_flight` when one is already running for this VPC, `503 not_ready`
while VPCs are not switched on in this deployment, and `503 address_allocator_busy`
with a `Retry-After` when the address allocator is busy with another request
(send the same request again). A retry with the same `Idempotency-Key` gets the first
answer back.

be deleted through this API; `409 vpc_not_empty` while subnets still hang off it, which
must be deleted first; `409 operation_in_flight` when another operation is already
running for it; `404` for a VPC that does not exist, is not yours, is filed under
another of your projects, or is already deleted; `503 not_ready` while VPCs are not
switched on in this deployment. A retry with the same `Idempotency-Key` gets the first
answer back.

are not switched on in this deployment.
